O.outcome_detail: visual and behavioral realism of the pedagogical agent

cells.quote: Compared with non-immersive media, pedagogical agents can be presented more realistically (i.e., high visual and behavioral realism of pedagogical agent) (Petersen et al., 2021), and the same applies to the learner’s virtual representation (high visual and behavioral realism of learner´s virtual representation) (Q. Cao et al., 2023).
cells.note: Conceptual framework claim; the study does not report a new empirical test of this contrast.

cells.quote: An earlier meta-analysis performed by Zheng et al. (2018) examined ten articles that evaluated the effect of a collaborative learning prototype on student performance in comparison to a non-immersive-based approach. Although the mean effect size advantage of 0.41 for XRCL (labelled VRCL in their article) was encouraging, the authors did not provide an overview of the included articles or information about sample sizes or the quality of the methods.
cells.note: The review reports a pooled mean effect size from ten articles but does not state the learners' expertise or age, settings, durations, knowledge types, or element interactivity; it also reports limitations in the meta-analysis's reporting of included articles, sample sizes, and methodological quality.

cells.quote: The results showed that all measures including self-presence, social presence, physical presence, enjoyment, entitativity (degree to which a collection of people is perceived as a single, unified entity; Campbell, 1958), and realism (perceived photorealism of the VR environment and people) increased over time, suggesting that the advantages of XRCL may increase as participants adapt to the medium and are no longer affected by the novelty of the technology (Han et al., 2022).
cells.note: The review reports a longitudinal increase across course meetings; no randomized treatment comparison or effect size is reported.

O.outcome_detail: misidentification or misclassification of simulation types

cells.quote: Carroll et al. [28] also showed that 70% of the related articles in medical digital simulation either ‘misidentified or misclassified’ simulation types, highlighting the ambiguity surrounding proper definitions.
cells.note: The 70% figure is reported secondarily by this scoping review as a finding attributed to Carroll et al.; the study text does not provide the underlying comparison, sample details, or an evaluative treatment effect.

cells.quote: A random-effects analysis of the GEARS scores showed that participants with extended reality had lower GEARS scores than those that were trained in extended reality. (Cohen’s d = −1.09, 95% CI [−3.17, 0.98]). However, this result is not statistically significant (P = 0.30)
cells.note: The comparison context in the study identifies the comparator as dry lab training; the quoted sentence contains an apparent wording error, repeating “extended reality” instead of “dry lab.”

cells.quote: A random-effects analysis was used for this meta-analysis and showed that participants with virtual reality training took statistically significant less time to complete tasks than participants with no additional training (Cohen’s d = −0.95, 95% CI [−1.73, −0.16], p = 0.02) (Fig. 2).
cells.note: The included participants were robotic novices, ranging from medical students to attending surgeons; the outcome was assessed after the training regimen.

O.outcome_detail: XR taxonomy features: immersion, stereoscopic vision, interaction, modification and haptic feedback

cells.quote: Finally, CS is an umbrella term used for computer-assisted simulation in general, which presents a digital training environment where stereoscopic vision and immersion are not available as objects are displayed in a single screen. Interaction of the user with digital objects is only provided through mouse, keyboard or touch screen manipulation, although haptic feedback might be present through simple force feedback devices [9, 36, 47, 116, 117, 118].
cells.note: This is a taxonomy distinction, not a comparative learning-effect estimate.

cells.quote: In both AR and AV, the virtual environment and/or objects can be manipulated and modified; what changes is the original environment that is being augmented [3, 16, 18, 20, 21, 24, 36, 37, 39, 44, 49, 50, 51, 53, 54, 55, 58, 60, 65, 66, 71, 74, 88, 90, 120, 121, 123, 124, 125, 126, 127, 128, 129, 130, 131, 132, 133, 134, 135, 136, 137].

cells.quote: Establishing a consensus on XR‐related terminology and definitions facilitates future research, allowing clear evidence reporting and analysis.

cells.quote: A random-effects analysis of time to complete showed a moderate, not statistically significant increase in time to complete for participants trained in virtual reality compared to participants trained in a dry lab (Cohen’s d = 0.65, 95% CI [−0.22,1.52], p = 0.14)
cells.note: The synthesis included randomized controlled and prospective studies of robotic novices; training involved extended-reality simulators versus inanimate physical dry-lab models.

cells.quote: Overall, 7 articles, involving a total of 428 participants, were included in this review. The findings indicate that XR can effectively reduce anxiety in midwifery and nursing education.
cells.note: The review included heterogeneous randomized, nonrandomized, controlled, and pre-post studies; findings included decreased anxiety, higher anxiety, and no significant difference.

cells.quote: Qualitative interviews suggested AR-CPR could be usable without device orientation, effective at cognitive offloading, and capable of reducing anxiety while boosting confidence.
cells.note: The study was an unblinded randomized crossover simulation; the anxiety finding came from qualitative interviews rather than a quantitative anxiety measure.

cells.quote: Results showed a significant 23.4% decrease in anxiety.

O.outcome_detail: live-patient operator performance and surgical outcomes

cells.quote: Two studies adopting the “XR vs. non-XR” design [62,69] and one of the longitudinal studies [19] tested, and successfully validated, the hypothesis that XR training of residents could improve outcomes on live-patient subjects when compared to residents that were not trained with XR.
cells.note: The review pooled three studies: two XR-versus-non-XR comparisons and one longitudinal study. It reported no printed effect size. Residents and clinical live-patient procedures indicate adult, intermediate-expertise learners in a workplace-clinical setting; duration varied across included studies.

cells.quote: Eight of 26 studies (31%) adopted an “XR vs. non-XR” controlled design, assessing and comparing UP between groups assigned to different conditions. The use of XR (VR in six cases and AR in two) was associated with improved UP and contributed to better outcomes.
cells.note: The review reports no pooled effect size.

O.outcome_detail: user-performance metrics in XR neurosurgical simulations

cells.quote: We found 16 studies that investigated performance differences based on level of training or experience (Table 3). Differences in UP favoring the more experienced participants were found in all studies except one [67]. As expected, these UP differences were not consistent across all metrics assessed [57,58,59,65], and there were outliers among the less experienced who clearly outperformed their peers, and at times, even their superiors [31,57].
cells.note: The review synthesized 16 empirical studies; the pooled pattern favored experienced participants overall but varied by metric, with occasional less-experienced outperformance.
